Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}\frac{9}{{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we use the identity $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡3x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}\frac{9}{{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}9{(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)})}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}9{sec}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =9{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}{sec}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=3x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=3x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{12}$ | $\frac{\pi }{9}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\pi }{4}$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}9{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}{sec}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =9{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{sec}^{2}⁡u\,\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{tan}⁡u{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3} \\  & =3(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})) \\  & =3(\sqrt{3}-1) \\  & =3\sqrt{3}-3.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0a251513-9691-50f6-b973-f2685262f1ed"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0a251513-9691-50f6-b973-f2685262f1ed" :answer-field/id #uuid "0a251513-9691-50f6-b973-f2685262f1ed" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-86a74f3d-6597-59e4-b81c-8406532b8b29" :answer-field/choices ["answer-86a74f3d-6597-59e4-b81c-8406532b8b29"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-86a74f3d-6597-59e4-b81c-8406532b8b29" :answer/id #uuid "86a74f3d-6597-59e4-b81c-8406532b8b29" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\sqrt{3}-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064857 :question/problem "$\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cot}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity ${cot}^{2}⁡x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cot}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {cot}^{2}⁡x+\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}+\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({csc}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186063198 :answer-field/correct "answer-f002d208-93d4-565e-847d-55497116f0c2" :answer-field/choices :question/worked-solution "We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cot}⁡x(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot 3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot 2\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot 3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot 2\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x-2\int \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2(-\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+C \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ec74a8fe-dc16-5d8a-9024-ad8266707d7b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}3\operatorname{sec}⁡2x{cos}^{2}⁡2x\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We use the identity $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}3\operatorname{sec}⁡2x{cos}^{2}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=2x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=2x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(sin\,(\frac{\pi }{3})-sin\,(0)) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5" :answer-field/id #uuid "d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c" :answer/id #uuid "4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-1a4cd24e-1cbf-547b-aab3-c78dc742ec94" :question/id #uuid "1a4cd24e-1cbf-547b-aab3-c78dc742ec94" :question/math-academy-id "q-114308" :question/problem "$\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{3}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{3}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}({tan}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that ${tan}^{2}⁡x=\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}$ to express this as

$$
\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-{sin}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{3}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-{sin}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {sin}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({sec}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-aca77544-0046-5524-9cef-1c8e548a94a1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We use the identities $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and $\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}-1\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5fe9e96d-c290-5de0-aea5-06fc2a18c7e7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5fe9e96d-c290-5de0-aea5-06fc2a18c7e7" :answer-field/id #uuid "5fe9e96d-c290-5de0-aea5-06fc2a18c7e7" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-e1161462-0f9d-545a-a5a5-27e6a35427ab" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e1161462-0f9d-545a-a5a5-27e6a35427ab"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e1161462-0f9d-545a-a5a5-27e6a35427ab" :answer/id #uuid "e1161462-0f9d-545a-a5a5-27e6a35427ab" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-8cd683e0-e43d-570b-a907-b426c76c1c6f" :question/id #uuid "8cd683e0-e43d-570b-a907-b426c76c1c6f" :question/math-academy-id "q-114319" :question/problem "${\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ to express this as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =-[\frac{1}{2}-1] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-07a0cda5-2de4-5cc2-802a-a5549d6da26a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id /6}\frac{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(1-{tan}^{2}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we use the fact that $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(1-{tan}^{2}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(1-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x})\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x})\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ to express this as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sec}^{2}⁡x\text{d}x.
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sec}^{2}⁡x\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{tan}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}-0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e803221b-b806-5450-a5a1-2379c91d357f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{1}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)}\frac{1}{u}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{1}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)} \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|1| \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)|.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-92469112-1ed0-55aa-bae5-7ad7d5ef9904"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{24}$ | $\frac{\pi }{8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /24}^{\pi /8}\operatorname{cot}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /24}^{\pi /8}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{4}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1" :answer-field/id #uuid "4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772" :answer/id #uuid "4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c26cdc41-d401-5858-96e0-ffa4a20294ca" :question/id #uuid "c26cdc41-d401-5858-96e0-ffa4a20294ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-49279" :question/problem "${\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "We use the identity $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,du={sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\sqrt{3}/3}^{\sqrt{3}}{u}^{2}\,\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}{|}_{\sqrt{3}/3}^{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({(\sqrt{3})}^{3}-{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3\sqrt{3}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{9}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}(3-\frac{1}{9}) \\  & =\frac{26\sqrt{3}}{27}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

$$
\int \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\text{d}x=\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,⟹\,-2\text{d}u=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}\,\text{d}x & =-2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})|+C\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e27fa184-c2a1-506b-ac6d-5109a0a21c79"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to calculate the integral

$$
\displaystyle \int\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

At first glance, this looks kind of tricky. However, if we use the identity $\dfrac{1}{\sin x} = \csc x,$ we can rewrite the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we see that this is just a standard trigonometric integral:

$$
\int\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\,\textrm d x  =  \int\csc^2 x\,\textrm d x =-\cot x + C
$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we use the identity $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡3x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}\frac{9}{{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}9{(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)})}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}9{sec}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =9{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}{sec}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=3x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=3x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{12}$ | $\frac{\pi }{9}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\pi }{4}$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}9{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}{sec}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =9{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{sec}^{2}⁡u\,\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{tan}⁡u{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3} \\  & =3(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})) \\  & =3(\sqrt{3}-1) \\  & =3\sqrt{3}-3.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0a251513-9691-50f6-b973-f2685262f1ed"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0a251513-9691-50f6-b973-f2685262f1ed" :answer-field/id #uuid "0a251513-9691-50f6-b973-f2685262f1ed" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-86a74f3d-6597-59e4-b81c-8406532b8b29" :answer-field/choices ["answer-86a74f3d-6597-59e4-b81c-8406532b8b29"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-86a74f3d-6597-59e4-b81c-8406532b8b29" :answer/id #uuid "86a74f3d-6597-59e4-b81c-8406532b8b29" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\sqrt{3}-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064857 :question/problem "$\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cot}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity ${cot}^{2}⁡x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x},$ as follows:

"Evaluate the following integral. ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}3\operatorname{sec}⁡2x{cos}^{2}⁡2x\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We use the identity $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}3\operatorname{sec}⁡2x{cos}^{2}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=2x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=2x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(sin\,(\frac{\pi }{3})-sin\,(0)) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5" :answer-field/id #uuid "d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c" :answer/id #uuid "4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-1a4cd24e-1cbf-547b-aab3-c78dc742ec94" :question/id #uuid "1a4cd24e-1cbf-547b-aab3-c78dc742ec94" :question/math-academy-id "q-114308" :question/problem "$\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{3}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{3}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}({tan}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that ${tan}^{2}⁡x=\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}$ to express this as

$$
\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-{sin}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{3}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-{sin}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {sin}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({sec}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-aca77544-0046-5524-9cef-1c8e548a94a1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We use the identities $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and $\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}-1\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5fe9e96d-c290-5de0-aea5-06fc2a18c7e7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5fe9e96d-c290-5de0-aea5-06fc2a18c7e7" :answer-field/id #uuid "5fe9e96d-c290-5de0-aea5-06fc2a18c7e7" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-e1161462-0f9d-545a-a5a5-27e6a35427ab" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e1161462-0f9d-545a-a5a5-27e6a35427ab"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e1161462-0f9d-545a-a5a5-27e6a35427ab" :answer/id #uuid "e1161462-0f9d-545a-a5a5-27e6a35427ab" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-8cd683e0-e43d-570b-a907-b426c76c1c6f" :question/id #uuid "8cd683e0-e43d-570b-a907-b426c76c1c6f" :question/math-academy-id "q-114319" :question/problem "${\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ to express this as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =-[\frac{1}{2}-1] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

Then, we use the fact that $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ as follows:

$$

$$

Now we use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ to express this as

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sec}^{2}⁡x\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{tan}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}-0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{24}$ | $\frac{\pi }{8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /24}^{\pi /8}\operatorname{cot}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /24}^{\pi /8}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{4}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1" :answer-field/id #uuid "4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772" :answer/id #uuid "4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c26cdc41-d401-5858-96e0-ffa4a20294ca" :question/id #uuid "c26cdc41-d401-5858-96e0-ffa4a20294ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-49279" :question/problem "${\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "We use the identity $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and rewrite the integral as

:tutorial/content "Suppose we want to calculate the integral

$$
\displaystyle \int\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

At first glance, this looks kind of tricky. However, if we use the identity $\dfrac{1}{\sin x} = \csc x,$ we can rewrite the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=2x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=2x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(sin\,(\frac{\pi }{3})-sin\,(0)) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-cdc94a5e-ffa3-5e3c-b067-8b7e71e5c799" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5" :answer-field/id #uuid "d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5"] ["answer-4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c" :answer/id #uuid "4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c"] ["answer-4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c" :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}"] ["answer-field-d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5" :answer-field/correct "answer-4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c"] ["answer-field-d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5" :answer-field/choices "answer-4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c"] ["question-cdc94a5e-ffa3-5e3c-b067-8b7e71e5c799" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5"] [17592186064225 :knowledge-point/questions "question-cdc94a5e-ffa3-5e3c-b067-8b7e71e5c799"] ["question-1a4cd24e-1cbf-547b-aab3-c78dc742ec94" :question/id #uuid "1a4cd24e-1cbf-547b-aab3-c78dc742ec94"] ["question-1a4cd24e-1cbf-547b-aab3-c78dc742ec94" :question/math-academy-id "q-114308"] ["question-1a4cd24e-1cbf-547b-aab3-c78dc742ec94" :question/problem "$\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{3}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$"] ["question-1a4cd24e-1cbf-547b-aab3-c78dc742ec94" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(1-{tan}^{2}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we use the fact that $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(1-{tan}^{2}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(1-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x})\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x})\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ to express this as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sec}^{2}⁡x\text{d}x.
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sec}^{2}⁡x\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{tan}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}-0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-49b73c78-3335-57b5-a631-c7f8dd771090" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e803221b-b806-5450-a5a1-2379c91d357f" :answer-field/id #uuid $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{1}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)}\frac{1}{u}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{1}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)} \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|1| \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)|.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a60367e9-cec6-56ff-bdf1-1a7368d63d95" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-92469112-1ed0-55aa-bae5-7ad7d5ef9904" :answer-field/id #uuid {{field-1}}"] ["question-dadcc805-1744-58ea-b449-313016666d23" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{24}$ | $\frac{\pi }{8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /24}^{\pi /8}\operatorname{cot}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /24}^{\pi /8}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dadcc805-1744-58ea-b449-313016666d23" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1" :answer-field/id #uuid "4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1"] ["answer-4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772" :answer/id #uuid "4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772"] ["answer-4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772" :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{4}"] ["answer-field-4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1" :answer-field/correct "answer-4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772"] ["answer-field-4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1" :answer-field/choices "answer-4afbb947-1a46-57c3-a2dc-395ab6315772"] ["question-dadcc805-1744-58ea-b449-313016666d23" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-4c69fd7b-4aa9-5d3d-a2cf-a03772cdb2a1"] [17592186064227 :knowledge-point/questions "question-dadcc805-1744-58ea-b449-313016666d23"] ["question-c26cdc41-d401-5858-96e0-ffa4a20294ca" :question/id #uuid "c26cdc41-d401-5858-96e0-ffa4a20294ca"] ["question-c26cdc41-d401-5858-96e0-ffa4a20294ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-49279"] ["question-c26cdc41-d401-5858-96e0-ffa4a20294ca" :question/problem "${\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$"] ["question-c26cdc41-d401-5858-96e0-ffa4a20294ca" :question/worked-solution "We use the identity $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,du={sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\sqrt{3}/3}^{\sqrt{3}}{u}^{2}\,\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}{|}_{\sqrt{3}/3}^{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({(\sqrt{3})}^{3}-{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3\sqrt{3}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{9}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}(3-\frac{1}{9}) \\  & =\frac{26\sqrt{3}}{27}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c26cdc41-d401-5858-96e0-ffa4a20294ca" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-82084fd2-bb79-5568-8b5b-a9fbb9530769" :answer-field/id #uuid $\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
\int \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\text{d}x=\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,⟹\,-2\text{d}u=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}\,\text{d}x & =-2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})|+C\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f01d9ac9-bb7d-5b0c-be19-2dc05bc65cd7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-e27fa184-c2a1-506b-ac6d-5109a0a21c79" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\displaystyle \int\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

At first glance, this looks kind of tricky. However, if we use the identity $\dfrac{1}{\sin x} = \csc x,$ we can rewrite the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we see that this is just a standard trigonometric integral:

$$
\int\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\,\textrm d x  =  \int\csc^2 x\,\textrm d x =-\cot x + C
$$

$$
\int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\,\textrm d x =  \int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{1}{\cos x}\cdot \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\dfrac{\sin x }{\cos x}  = \tan x$ and $\dfrac{1}{\cos x} = \sec x$ to express this as

$$
\int_0^{\pi/3} \sec x\tan x\,\textrm d x,
$$

which is a standard trigonometric integral. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064858 :question/id #uuid "c589cab7-d081-524b-ae47-ab787d74dcb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-49273"} {:db/id 17592186064859 :question/id #uuid :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}=\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ to express this as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cot}⁡x(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\int (\operatorname{cot}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(-\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+C \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186250238 :question/id #uuid "062977fc-037b-5a67-9a07-c0d038a63f3e" :question/math-academy-id "q-114318"} {:db/id 17592186321044 :question/id #uuid \tan{2x}\,\textrm d x.$" :question/worked-solution "We use the identity $\tan 2x = \dfrac{\sin 2x}{\cos 2x}$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
\int \tan{2x}\,\textrm d x = \int \dfrac{\sin{2x}}{\cos 2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Notice that the numerator of the integrand is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we can solve this by substitution.

Let $u=\cos 2x.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-2 \sin 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac 1 2 \,\textrm d u= \sin 2x \, \textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡2x|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)^{-1}|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡2x|+C\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050489} {:db/id 17592186064673 :question/id #uuid "1fabab33-132f-500c-992f-45cbf132915e" :question/math-academy-id "q-2622"} {:db/id 17592186064856 :question/id #uuid "eeffd6d0-ba71-5af0-8a18-c001ad19ba1e" :question/math-academy-id "q-49259"} {:db/id 17592186250228 :question/id #uuid "de415510-24b2-53a0-b8c3-ddc9cdee62b2" :question/math-academy-id "q-114294"} {:db/id 17592186319212 :question/id #uuid "0a9ebacf-0ee8-5c1e-ba6d-9dd55f05b2b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-347941"} {:db/id 17592186321040 :question/id #uuid "313e0a29-ace7-5c0c-a6d4-e0a9a2fe5bcd" :question/math-academy-id "q-352786"} {:db/id 17592186321041 :question/id #uuid "00fe6411-9f3d-58f9-a531-7305d81e2e57" :question/math-academy-id "q-352797" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064227 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7d309fd9-62bd-5307-9dfc-128f9ff028aa" :knowledge-point/title "Integrating a Trigonometric Expression Using Identities and Substitution"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3c4c17b5-6041-5b4a-921e-16d5b13a2a5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}(\frac{3}{2})" :db/id 17592186319573}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "3c4c17b5-6041-5b4a-921e-16d5b13a2a5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}(\frac{3}{2})" :db/id 17592186319573} :answer-field/id #uuid "786408a1-4911-5c78-8041-0f51f924f24b" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186320413}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{12}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{3/2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{1}^{3/2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186321042 :question/id #uuid "07713ce3-1f95-5769-81d0-a1d74de4220e" :question/math-academy-id "q-352798"} {:db/id 17592186323768 :question/id #uuid 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.
This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.
On completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.
Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.
Students will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.
The course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.
A solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.
Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.
Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.
On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.
Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.
The course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning
